messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a large live capture dataset from badgers that I have been working with in secr 3.1.3. The occasions and captures by session are shown below. I am wondering if recaptures are too sparse and perhaps that is contributing to the problem in the most recent model I attempted.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-34r0c24ZhWo/WphGUX-SHMI/AAAAAAAAPXI/_rBaiBzQm0w_MmDUEkcv0xql08cMtq1fQCLcBGAs/s1600/Capture.PNG>

A model of D~1, g0~b, sigma~1 produced an estimate of ~0.8/km^2, which is reasonable for this population. But a model of D~1, g0~k, sigma~1 took substantially longer to fit (2 days) and produced a density estimate of 1.1*10^10/ha! There were also clearly problems with estimating other parameters. There was an "at least one variance calculation failed" warning produced, and numerous NA likelihood estimates throughout. Some of the output is shown below.

Hello,

I am trying to bring in multiple rasters to add covariates to my mask, but I am having issues with my second raster (which is a DEM elevation model). My first raster is classified habitat data with codes for various habitat types, and I have no trouble running a model with this data (which I did not include here due to the very large file size of the rasters):

###Load and Prepare SECR capture history
lsCH <- read.capthist('lscapt.txt', 'lstrap.txt', detector = 'count', covnames = c("sex"))

#2km habitat mask
lsmask_2km <- make.mask(traps, buffer = 15000, spacing = 2000, type = "trapbuffer")
#Loading Raster
ls_hab <- raster("LittleSmoky_Hab_30m.tif", verbose=FALSE)
#turn to polygon, secr doens't like raster
hab_poly <- as(ls_hab, "SpatialGridDataFrame")
##rename columns
names(hab_poly) <- "hab"
###Add hab values to mask
LS_2km_mask <- addCovariates(lsmask_2km, hab_poly)

##Model NULL
ls.fit.NULL.2km <- secr.fit(lsCH,mask=LS_2km_mask, trace=FALSE, method = 'Nelder-Mead')
##Model D~habitat
ls.fit.D.hab.2km <- secr.fit(lsCH,mask=LS_2km_mask,model=list(D~hab), trace=FALSE, method = 'Nelder-Mead')

#Loading Raster
ls_elev <- raster("LittleSmoky_Elevation.tif", verbose=FALSE)

I have two questions regarding the interpretation:
Are sigma values comparable to home ranges or average movements obtained through other methods? i.e. distances between detections, telemetry data, total distance moved
Is sigma the distance from the activity center in any direction in the stream network (i.e. total home range might be sigma × 2 if the stream has no branching), the total distance (sigma if the stream has no branching), or something else?
Any insight would be appreciated. Thank you,
-Wendy

Hi
I cannot see what is going on here.It's not necessary to match extents or resolution, except that obviously the data source should cover all mask cells, nor do I know of anything special about elevation models. Of the three masks in the RData file you attached, only one has a covariate and that is not 'elev'. I suggest focussing on getting the mask right before fitting any model. I know that's what you're trying to do, but dig deeper with checks like
head(covariates(LS_2km_mask))
table(covariates(LS_2km_mask)$hab)
plot(LS_2km_mask, covariate = 'hab', xy='bottomright')

(My impression is that your habitat types are highly interspersed: every feasible home range will include nearly the same mix of types, so type is unlikely to be predictive of density.  Using numeric codes for habitat classes is dangerous: convert to factor. And I am almost certain you cannot have enough data or patience to fit 10 levels, most of which relate to very small areas.)
Murray

On Saturday, March 24, 2018 at 7:37:43 AM UTC+13, Wendy Leuenberger wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I'm working with secrlinear to model stream-dwelling species. I'm trying to understand the sigma parameter that represents movement. In the secrlinear vignette, this parameter is described as the spatial scale of detection, spatial scale of animal movement, or an index of home-range size.
>

The vignette says "...secrlinear uses \sigma as the parameter to represent the spatial scale of detection. For many purposes \sigma may also be interpreted as the spatial scale of animal movements, or an index of home-range size.  However, ..." which is not quite what you indicate. Sigma is the parameter for the spatial scale of detection; other meanings are secondary, with lots of ifs and buts.

> I have two questions regarding the interpretation:
> Are sigma values comparable to home ranges or average movements obtained through other methods? i.e. distances between detections, telemetry data, total distance moved

"comparable" in a sense, but maybe not the one you mean

> Is sigma the distance from the activity center in any direction in the stream network (i.e. total home range might be sigma × 2 if the stream has no branching), the total distance (sigma if the stream has no branching), or something else?

Sigma relates to minimum distance along the network from the activity centre; I think you've got that. It does make for complications when there is dense branching, as explained in the vignette. For total range length I think you mean x 4 not x 2 (by analogy with +/- 2 SD for 95% of normal distribution? I'm not rushing to endorse any of your interpretations, but at least _if_ activity is normally distributed, and activity relates directly to detection probability (no behavioural oddities like latrines at edge of range), and the stream is unbranched, and you're OK with 95% then 4sigma does it.

Basically, you always have to have your wits about you when interpreting sigma as a measure of home-range size, and there are issues in linear networks (length of stream within sigma of a centre point depends on the intensity of branching) that do not arise in 2-D.

> Any insight would be appreciated. Thank you,
> -Wendy

messages.subject: Study design over large region
messages.body_plain:
I’m new to secr models, so sorry for the pretty basic question, but I’ve been tasked with creating a study design for a large region (85,500 km2) that is capable of estimating the density of black bears in Wisconsin. Thankfully, there are several insightful papers that studied the influence of trap spacing and trap configurations on density estimates. We will likely use a clustered approach with 4-6 hair snares spaced 1 -3 km apart within the cluster. As of now, the idea is to systematically survey the region by spacing the centers of each cluster approximately 14-20 km apart. We are conducting a pilot season in May in one county (3,201 km2) to determine whether this is feasible.

To determine the best trap configuration, I’m running simulations to evaluate the relative bias and relative standard errors of the different trap configurations using an estimated density (.37 bears/km2), sigma (1-km), and probability of detection (0.2) with 5 or 6 occasions, but is there something else I should be paying attention too when designing a large-scale project? Reading about these models, it seems as if they can take quite a bit of computational power, and I’m wondering if having >350 clusters of 4-6 traps will be too computationally expensive? Alternatively, would it be best to set snares in proportion to the distribution of habitat (similar to Sun et. al. 2017) or alter spacing based on whether the area is designated as primary or secondary range?

Thanks for any feedback!

Laura

messages.subject: Re: Study design over large region
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura

I like the ambition! I would say that you have more than a basic problem.

Looking on the dark side, I don't think there is a reliable source for the design of large spatial surveys using SECR. As you imply, a lot might be gained by stratified sampling (putting more effort where we expect more bears). The principles of stratification transfer from other spatial sampling, but care is needed in the SECR modelling when effort is stratified.

For systematic designs I don't think bias is an issue for SECR as long as you avoid designs with pathological spacing (cluster << home range size, within-cluster spacing > home range diameter) (of course if your spatial sampling is not representative you will get the wrong answer). The real question is how to maximise precision for a given level of effort. Precision depends on the total number of 'recaptures' (redetections of bears) which can be predicted without simulation in 'secrdesign'.

The computation demands with >350 x 6 detectors (these are hair snags, right, not traps) are large but not unmanageable, and that should not put you off.  There are shortcuts (e.g. 'mashing' in secr) if all clusters use the same configuration. At the worst, you could carve the survey area up into subregions analysed separately.

I'm sceptical of your pilot values. I do not believe there are 0.37 black bears per sq km across half of Wisconsin. sigma = 1 km is small, and overall detection probability scales with sigma^2, so this is a sensitive issue. Remember sigma is likely to vary inversely with density (sigma approx 0.6 / sqrt(D) which does neatly fit your D,sigma). By 'probability of detection' I guess you mean the intercept of the detection function, but this is a misnomer: probability of detection is determined by the intercept (g0, lambda0, p0) and sigma together. p0=g0=0.2 sounds high, but that depends entirely on the time interval (length of an 'occasion').

Murray
